question: A 10-day-old neonate presents with fever, bulging fontanelle, and poor feeding. Lumbar puncture shows turbid CSF with neutrophilic pleocytosis, very high protein, and low glucose. Which organism is the MOST likely causative agent for bacterial meningitis at this age?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Neisseria meningitidis is the most common organism in older children and adolescents (5–19 years), not in neonates.
Streptococcus pneumoniae predominates in children aged 1 month to 5 years and in adults, not in the neonatal period.
GBS (Streptococcus agalactiae), along with E. coli and Listeria monocytogenes, is the leading cause of neonatal meningitis (0–28 days). GBS is acquired from the maternal genital tract.
Hib was previously a major cause in unimmunised children aged 2 months to 5 years; it is very rare in neonates and has declined dramatically with vaccination.

overallFeedback.feedback: Recall the age-stratified organism spectrum: neonates (0–28 days) → GBS, E. coli, Listeria; infants/young children (1 month–5 years) → S. pneumoniae, N. meningitidis; older children and adolescents → N. meningitidis and S. pneumoniae.

Correct. Neonatal meningitis (0–28 days) is dominated by GBS, E. coli, and Listeria — organisms acquired perinatally. The empiric regimen for this age group is ampicillin plus an aminoglycoside (or a third-generation cephalosporin), not ceftriaxone alone.
